newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault to axe jobs in France, too.
newsitem.headline: Renault to axe jobs in France, too.

text.p: Renault SA, facing big losses and shrinking demand for its vehicles, told its employees Tuesday that it planned to cut 2,764 jobs in France this year in addition to a fiercely contested plant closure in Belgium.

Angry union leaders warned the company it could face a long labour conflict over the cuts, while a senior politician accused Renault Chairman Louis Schweitzer of acting too swiftly and called for negotiations.

The job cut plan for France followed an announcement last Thursday that Renault would close a plant near Brussels in June, with the direct loss of 3,100 jobs and another 1,000 put at risk at supplying companies.
Renault has a total workforce of 140,000.
A Renault spokeswoman declined comment on the cuts but said a staff committee would be meeting March 13 to discuss an "employment plan" in France.

The plan would include "both a labour restructuring with internal transfers and the elimination of posts, as well as measures aimed at youth employment, with new recruitment to make up for early retirements," she said.

The cuts, if carried through, would be the biggest by the partially privatised company since it shed 3,700 jobs in 1992, when it was still state-owned. The French government still retains a 46 percent stake.
Renault's unions have called a one-hour strike Friday in all plants in France, Belgium and Spain to protest the shutdown of the Belgian factory.

Senior government parliamentarian Michel Pericard criticised the way the Belgium plant closing decision was announced and urged Schweitzer to open negotiations with the workforce and the government on an early retirement plan that was rejected by the Industry Ministry last week.

Renault officials rejected the criticism, saying there was no "nice way" to break such news and insisting the job cuts, which they said had been delayed due to the slow privatisation process, were vital to make Renault competitive.

Renault, privatised in stages in 1994 and 1996, is expected to announce on March 20 a 1996 operating loss of more than two billion francs ($347 million) as well as a big charge for the Belgian restructuring and possibly other job cuts.
